name: Learn: Services & Networking
objective: CKAD › Services & Networking (20%). Goal: expose workloads with ClusterIP and NodePort Services, route HTTP with an Ingress host/path rule, lock traffic down with a default-deny NetworkPolicy, and debug a Service that has no endpoints — the connectivity tasks the exam leans on.
description: Learn how traffic reaches your pods, step by step — ClusterIP and NodePort Services, an Ingress host/path rule, a default-deny NetworkPolicy, and how to debug a Service whose selector doesn't match its pods. Every step is graded on the full correct result.

questions.title: ClusterIP Service with endpoints
questions.teach:
A **Service** gives a stable virtual IP + DNS name in front of a set of pods. A Service finds its pods with a **selector** (label match); for each matching, *ready* pod it creates an endpoint. DNS name is `<svc>.<ns>.svc.cluster.local`.

**Ports** (keep these straight):
- `port` — what the Service itself listens on (cluster-internal).
- `targetPort` — the container port traffic is forwarded to (may be a name, not just a number).
- `nodePort` — only for NodePort/LoadBalancer, the port opened on every node.

**Service types:**
- **ClusterIP** (default) — internal-only virtual IP.
- **NodePort** — ClusterIP + a port on every node; also has a ClusterIP.
- **LoadBalancer** — NodePort + an external LB; also has a ClusterIP + NodePort.
- **ExternalName** — no selector/IP, returns a CNAME to an external DNS name.
- **Headless** (`clusterIP: None`) — no virtual IP; DNS returns pod IPs directly (StatefulSets).

Other knobs: `sessionAffinity: ClientIP` (sticky by client IP); a **selector-less** Service lets you manage **EndpointSlices** (or the legacy Endpoints object) by hand to point at external IPs.

**GOTCHAS:**
- Empty `kubectl get endpoints <svc>` = selector matches no ready pod → dead end (selector typo, wrong labels, or pods not Ready).
- `targetPort` defaults to `port` if omitted — easy to forget when they differ.
- `kubectl expose` copies the workload's selector for you but can't pin a `nodePort` or set a headless clusterIP.
questions.prompt:
A Deployment `web` (3 replicas, label `app=web`, container port 8080) is already running in namespace `svcnet-learn`. Create a ClusterIP Service named `web` that selects `app=web`, with `port` 80 forwarding to `targetPort` 8080.

Target: `kubectl -n svcnet-learn get endpoints web` lists 3 endpoint addresses.
questions.hint: `kubectl -n svcnet-learn expose deployment web --name=web --port=80 --target-port=8080` — expose copies the Deployment's `app=web` selector for you. Check with `kubectl -n svcnet-learn get endpoints web`.
questions.solution:
kubectl -n svcnet-learn expose deployment web --name=web --port=80 --target-port=8080
kubectl -n svcnet-learn get svc web
kubectl -n svcnet-learn get endpoints web   # should list 3 addresses

verification.description: Service web is ClusterIP, port 80 -> targetPort 8080, with 3 endpoints

questions.title: NodePort Service on a pinned port
questions.teach:
A **NodePort** Service builds on ClusterIP: it additionally opens the same port on **every node**, so `<nodeIP>:<nodePort>` reaches the pods. A NodePort therefore *also* has a ClusterIP (and a LoadBalancer has both a ClusterIP and a NodePort).

The three ports in play:
- `port` — the ClusterIP port (internal).
- `targetPort` — the container port.
- `nodePort` — the port on each node, **must be 30000–32767**.

**Ways to create it:**
- Manifest with `type: NodePort` and `nodePort:` under the port entry (the only way to *pin* the value cleanly).
- `kubectl expose ... --type=NodePort` (Kubernetes auto-assigns the nodePort) then `patch`/`edit` to pin it.

**GOTCHAS:**
- A `nodePort` outside 30000–32767 is rejected.
- If you don't set `nodePort`, Kubernetes picks a random one — the exam usually wants a *specific* value, so pin it.
- `kubectl expose` alone can't pin a `nodePort`; you must patch/edit or write YAML.
- Still needs a matching selector + ready pods, or there are no endpoints behind the open port.
questions.prompt:
In `svcnet-learn`, create a NodePort Service named `web-np` selecting `app=web`, with `port` 80, `targetPort` 8080, and `nodePort` pinned to **30080**.

Target: `kubectl -n svcnet-learn get svc web-np` shows type NodePort with node port 30080.
questions.hint: Easiest is a manifest: `type: NodePort`, and under `ports` set `port: 80`, `targetPort: 8080`, `nodePort: 30080`. Or `kubectl expose deployment web --name=web-np --type=NodePort --port=80 --target-port=8080` then `kubectl -n svcnet-learn patch svc web-np -p '{"spec":{"ports":[{"port":80,"targetPort":8080,"nodePort":30080}]}}'`.
questions.solution:
cat <<'EOF' | kubectl apply -f -
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: web-np
  namespace: svcnet-learn
spec:
  type: NodePort
  selector:
    app: web
  ports:
  - port: 80
    targetPort: 8080
    nodePort: 30080
EOF
kubectl -n svcnet-learn get svc web-np

verification.description: Service web-np is NodePort with nodePort 30080 -> targetPort 8080 and has endpoints

questions.title: Ingress host + path rule
questions.teach:
An **Ingress** provides HTTP(S) routing from outside — matching on **host** and **path** and forwarding to a backend Service. An Ingress rule names the backend Service and the Service **port** (the Service's `port`, *not* the pod's targetPort).

**pathType** (required on each path):
- `Prefix` — matches the path and everything under it (`/` matches all).
- `Exact` — matches the exact path only.
- `ImplementationSpecific` — delegates matching to the controller.

**Other pieces:**
- `ingressClassName` — which controller handles it (replaces the old `kubernetes.io/ingress.class` annotation).
- `defaultBackend` — catches requests that match no rule.
- **TLS** — `spec.tls[]` references a `kubernetes.io/tls` Secret (`tls.crt`/`tls.key`) per host.
- Multiple hosts and multiple paths per host are allowed.

**GOTCHAS:**
- An Ingress does nothing without a running **ingress controller** — the object can exist and route nothing. (No controller runs in this bench, so grading checks the Ingress object's rule — host, path, backend service + port — not live HTTP.)
- Backend port = the **Service** port (name or number), not the container targetPort.
- `kubectl create ingress --rule="host/path*=svc:port"` uses `*` to mean `pathType: Prefix`; omit the `*` for `Exact`.
questions.prompt:
In `svcnet-learn`, create an Ingress named `web-ing` with one rule: host `web.example.com`, path `/` (pathType `Prefix`), routing to Service `web` on port 80.

Target: `kubectl -n svcnet-learn get ingress web-ing` exists with that host/path/backend.
questions.hint: `kubectl -n svcnet-learn create ingress web-ing --rule="web.example.com/*=web:80"` creates host web.example.com, pathType Prefix, backend web:80 in one line.
questions.solution:
kubectl -n svcnet-learn create ingress web-ing --rule="web.example.com/*=web:80"
kubectl -n svcnet-learn get ingress web-ing -o yaml

verification.description: Ingress web-ing routes host web.example.com path / to service web:80

questions.title: Default-deny ingress NetworkPolicy
questions.teach:
By default every pod is **non-isolated** — it accepts traffic from everywhere. A **NetworkPolicy** makes the *selected* pods isolated for the listed `policyTypes`. Only enforced by a CNI that supports it.

**Structure:**
- `podSelector: {}` — empty = **all pods** in the namespace; a label selector = just those pods.
- `policyTypes: [Ingress]`, `[Egress]`, or both — you only isolate the directions you list.
- `ingress`/`egress` rules with `from`/`to` peers + `ports`.

**Default-deny patterns:** list the direction in `policyTypes` with **no** matching rules → nothing allowed that way. (This step: `podSelector: {}` + `policyTypes: [Ingress]` + no `ingress:` key.)

**Peer selectors (the classic trap):**
- `podSelector` + `namespaceSelector` in the **same** `from`/`to` element = **AND** (pods matching both).
- The same two in **separate** list elements = **OR**.
- `ipBlock` with `cidr` (and optional `except`) for IP ranges.

**GOTCHAS:**
- Policies are **additive** and allow-only — there is no "deny" rule; you deny by *not* allowing.
- A default-deny **egress** policy blocks **DNS** (kube-system, port 53 **UDP and TCP**) — add an egress allow for DNS or everything breaks.
- `policyTypes` controls which directions are isolated; always list every direction you intend to restrict (don't rely on implicit behaviour).
- NetworkPolicies are namespaced and never span namespaces except via `namespaceSelector`.
questions.prompt:
In `svcnet-learn`, create a NetworkPolicy named `default-deny` that selects **all** pods in the namespace and denies **all ingress** traffic.

Target: `kubectl -n svcnet-learn get networkpolicy default-deny` exists with an empty podSelector, policyTypes `[Ingress]`, and no ingress rules.
questions.hint: Manifest with `spec.podSelector: {}`, `spec.policyTypes: [Ingress]`, and no `ingress:` key at all (an empty/absent rule list = deny all).
questions.solution:
cat <<'EOF' | kubectl apply -f -
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: NetworkPolicy
metadata:
  name: default-deny
  namespace: svcnet-learn
spec:
  podSelector: {}
  policyTypes:
  - Ingress
EOF
kubectl -n svcnet-learn get networkpolicy default-deny -o yaml

verification.description: NetworkPolicy default-deny: empty podSelector, Ingress policyType, no ingress rules

questions.title: Fix a Service with no endpoints
questions.teach:
The #1 reason a Service doesn't work: its **selector doesn't match any pod labels**, so `kubectl get endpoints` (or `get endpointslices`) is empty and requests go nowhere.

**Debug flow:**
1. `kubectl get endpoints <svc>` — empty?
2. Compare `kubectl get svc <svc> -o jsonpath='{.spec.selector}'` with `kubectl get pods --show-labels`.
3. Fix the mismatch: `kubectl patch`/`edit` the Service selector, or relabel the pods.

**But "no endpoints" has other causes too — check all of them:**
- Pods exist and match, but are **not Ready** (failing readiness probe) → excluded from endpoints.
- `targetPort` names a container port the pod doesn't expose.
- Wrong namespace (Service and pods in different namespaces).
- A **selector-less** Service that's missing its manual EndpointSlice/Endpoints.

**GOTCHAS:**
- Only **Ready** pods become endpoints — a crash-looping or unready pod silently disappears from the Service.
- Editing `spec.selector` is live and immediate; no pod restart needed.
- `kubectl describe svc <svc>` shows the resolved Endpoints line — fastest sanity check.
questions.prompt:
A Service `api` in `svcnet-learn` has **no endpoints** — its selector is `app=api-WRONG` but the backing pods (Deployment `api`) are labelled `app=api`. Fix the Service's selector so it matches, and endpoints populate.

Target: `kubectl -n svcnet-learn get endpoints api` lists at least 1 address.
questions.hint: `kubectl -n svcnet-learn get pods --show-labels` to see the real label (`app=api`), then `kubectl -n svcnet-learn patch svc api -p '{"spec":{"selector":{"app":"api"}}}'`. Re-check endpoints.
questions.solution:
kubectl -n svcnet-learn get endpoints api          # empty
kubectl -n svcnet-learn get pods --show-labels     # app=api
kubectl -n svcnet-learn patch svc api -p '{"spec":{"selector":{"app":"api"}}}'
kubectl -n svcnet-learn get endpoints api          # now populated

verification.description: Service api selector fixed to app=api and endpoints now populate
